Phases

All-phase hiatus

SPTCal Guide

Fill in the panel on the left and the schedule builds itself in the preview. Everything below explains what each control does and how the calendar is calculated. Nothing you enter leaves your computer.

Show Info

Title names the project. It appears in the printed Excel header and becomes the file name when you export or save (e.g. “Show Title - Season 1 Planning Calendar.xlsx”).

Shooting Days per Episode is informational context for the shoot — it’s shown in the header’s production summary. The actual shoot length is driven by the total shooting-day count you set on the Production phase.

Phases

Each phase is a block of the schedule — Writer’s Room, Pre-Prep, Prod Prep, Production, and Post are provided by default, each with its own color. For every phase you set:

  • Start date — any date snaps to the Monday of that week (weeks always run Monday–Sunday).
  • Duration — in weeks for most phases. Production is special: it’s measured in shooting days, not weeks, and is scheduled day-by-day (see Union holidays below). Its total isn’t typed — it’s the sum of the episodes, which come from Show Info.
  • Name — click the phase name to rename it; the label carries through to every week of that phase and to the export.
  • Color — click the little color square to the left of any phase name (built-in or custom) to pick from the standard palette. The choice applies everywhere: the Waterfall, the Month view, and the export.
  • Phase hiatus — turn on the toggle under any phase (e.g. “Writer’s Rm Hiatus”) to pause just that phase for a set number of weeks from a chosen Monday. It works like the all-phase hiatus — the phase still delivers its full requested weeks — but the pause stays in that phase’s own column and never widens into the others. Its name box and color square, under the toggle, label and color every week of the pause, in both views and every export; double-click its band in the Waterfall to go straight to them. With Ripple Hiatus Periods on (in Settings › Preferences › Hiatus), every other phase that starts on or after it moves by the same weeks (see below).

+ Add phase creates a custom phase with its own name, color, start, and length. Phases can overlap — when two or more run in the same week, the preview and export add columns so they sit side by side. Columns follow a clear rule: the earliest-starting phase takes the leftmost column and keeps it, later overlapping phases sit to its right, and non-overlapping phases share a column to keep the sheet narrow. When only one phase is running in a week, it spans across the empty columns so there are no blank gaps.

Header (Auto, Template, Manual or Off). The calendar header has nine lines and three modes, and it can be turned Off; the Header button in the toolbar above the preview says which one you are in and opens a menu to change it. The Month view’s header has its own mode, and the button follows whichever view is showing. In Manual mode a formatting bar sits above the header. Auto fills every line from your inputs (title, production span, Principal Photography dates, episode count, and the Version you type in Show info) and keeps them up to date — the lines are not editable. Template lets you write the lines yourself and put live data in them: {version}, {production.wrap}, {episodes} and so on. Click into a line to see its tokens; click away and it shows the result again. Use Insert ▾ in the formatting bar to see everything available. Anything in square brackets disappears when the data inside it is missing, so [{episodes} Episodes] shows nothing at all until you enter an episode count. Manual is plain text you type, and nothing in it updates itself — braces are printed literally there. Switching Template → Manual freezes the current values and removes the tokens; switching to Auto discards your lines entirely. Off hides the header in that view and gives its space to the calendar: the PDF prints none, nor does Excel from the Waterfall view. Choosing Template or Manual again brings back the lines you had. Every switch is a single undo.

Header presets. Settings → Presets saves the whole arrangement — all nine lines and their formatting — under a name, and applies it to any calendar in one click. Presets stay on your computer and are never part of a saved calendar, so sending someone a .sptcal sends the header it is wearing but not your library. Use Export… and Import preset file… to move one between machines or send it to a colleague. A preset stores the tokens, never the values they happen to show today, which is why saving one is only offered in Template mode.

Episodes

Tick a Season, fill in Shooting Days per Episode and Number of Episodes in Show Info, and the episode list builds itself under Production — named by the usual convention (season 1 gives 101, 102…; season 4 gives 401, 402…). Each episode is named “Episode 101”, and its bar in the month view reads “Shoot 101”. Rename an episode and its bar reads the new name exactly. When two or more seasons share the calendar, tick them all: the header names every one (“S3 & S4”), and the episodes number from the first. Until those three are filled in, Production can’t be scheduled and its row is greyed out.

Production’s Total Shooting Days is the sum of the episode list, so it’s shown rather than typed. Change any episode’s day count and the total follows — eight 8‑day episodes is 64 shooting days, but bump one to 10 and it becomes 66. Everything downstream — the Waterfall view, the Excel export, the day-by-day scheduling around weekends, holidays and hiatus — works off that single number exactly as before.

Episodes are added and removed only by changing Number of Episodes. Lowering it removes episodes from the end; if one of those had been edited by hand, the panel says so rather than dropping it silently. In Month view the episodes replace Production’s bar, laid across its shooting days back to back — so an episode can end mid‑week and the next start the same week.

Union holidays

Schedule effect — Production only. Pick a Production Region in Show info (it is also in Settings → Region, with the holiday list) and, if a recognized union holiday lands on what would have been a shoot day, that day is skipped and the shoot extends day-by-day until the full shooting-day count is met. Holidays never change any other phase’s dates. Un-ticking a holiday’s Enable box in that list drops it from this show entirely, so it stops costing a shoot day; you can also add your own single-day holidays, which is something the week-based hiatus rows can’t express.

Which holidays these are. The United States has two lists, each of eleven recognized holidays (Juneteenth was added effective 1 January 2025). U.S. Area Standards covers everywhere but New York — the West Coast Studio Local Agreements and the Area Standards Agreement carry an identical list, so Los Angeles, Atlanta and Albuquerque are the same. Type the town in Show info’s Location to have it shown. Note that Columbus Day is not included anywhere (it is on no IATSE calendar) and Veterans Day is not an Area Standards holiday (outside New York it appears only in the AICP commercial contract), so treating either as a no-shoot day outside New York would wrongly cost you shoot days.

New York is the US exception. Its crews (IATSE Local 52, shooting in New York or New Jersey) and its drivers (Teamsters Local 817) have the same list, which swaps Good Friday for Veterans Day — same count, different days. (Martin Luther King Jr. Day was added to Local 52 effective 1 January 2023.) So pick New York for a New York or New Jersey shoot and U.S. Area Standards for everywhere else.

Canada is chosen by province, because the statutory lists really do diverge: Boxing Day is Ontario-only among the provinces listed; Remembrance Day applies in BC and Alberta but not Ontario or Quebec; the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation is statutory in BC and Manitoba (in Ontario the IATSE Local 873 agreement treats it as a “Proclaimed Holiday” instead); and the Fête nationale (St-Jean-Baptiste, 24 June) is Quebec-only. Quebec is also the exception where either Good Friday or Easter Monday is required — the tool lists Good Friday, so switch it manually if your production observes Easter Monday instead. Nova Scotia is the shortest list: Victoria Day, Thanksgiving and Boxing Day are not statutory paid holidays there.

Weekend holidays. A holiday landing on a Saturday or Sunday also generates an “(Observed)” weekday entry, since that substitute day is the one that actually costs a shoot day. The US follows the IATSE rule (Saturday → the preceding Friday, Sunday → the following Monday); Canada and the UK move forward to the next free weekday, so a Saturday Christmas plus a Sunday Boxing Day become Monday and Tuesday rather than colliding. Always check these against your own union agreement before relying on them — and note that Christmas Eve and New Year’s Eve are not holidays (in BC they carry premium pay, but they are working days).

Notes display — all phases. Every holiday that lands inside any phase is logged in the Notes column with its date. Use the per-holiday checklist under Union holidays to choose which appear in each view — display only, this doesn’t change the schedule. By default none show in the Waterfall and all show in the Month calendar.

Changing the Region asks first once you’ve edited notes. A new Region recomputes Production’s dates, because its shoot skips a different set of holidays, so a note you wrote beside a shoot day can end up beside the wrong day. While a note, a note’s colour or a hiatus band has been edited (and Production is scheduled), picking another Region asks before it changes anything: Continue switches, and Cancel keeps the Region you had.

Simultaneous post

The Simultaneous Post checkbox sits under the Production phase, since that’s what it’s measured against: tick it to mark weeks where post runs concurrently with the shoot, and the offset field beneath sets how many calendar weeks after Production begins the flag starts — a hiatus inside that stretch still counts toward it. A flagged week shows its marker tucked into the leftmost free column right beside the running phase, so it takes as little space as possible.

The “Number these weeks & continue Post’s count” checkbox beneath chooses how those weeks are labelled and counted. Off (the default), every flagged week simply reads “Simultaneous Post” and the Post phase counts independently, starting at Post wk 1. Switch it on and they read “Simultaneous Post wk n” and count as post weeks — so if two run concurrently (wk 1–2), the regular Post phase picks up where they left off at Post wk 3.

To call it something else, type a name in the box at the top of its settings (“Sim Post”, say). The new name shows in both views and every export, and numbered weeks read “name wk n”. Clear the box to go back to “Simultaneous Post”.

All-phase hiatus

Ripple Hiatus Periods (on unless you turn it off). When you add, remove, lengthen, shorten or move a hiatus, every phase that starts on or after it moves by the same number of weeks, so the gaps between phases stay as they were. Like Shift, it counts working weeks: a phase whose start crosses a locked hiatus moves that hiatus’s length further. Moving a hiatus counts as taking it out where it was and putting it back where it is now. A change to Weeks moves them the moment you make it. A start date moves them once you finish it (pick it in the calendar, press Enter, or leave the box), so a date half typed never moves anything. A line under the hiatus says what moved. Notes and unlocked hiatuses after it travel too; locked hiatuses, holidays and notes with a date stay put. One ⌘Z takes back the push and keeps your change. The switch is in Settings › Preferences › Hiatus, and it stays on this computer. Off, a hiatus only pauses the phases running through it.

Add one or more hiatus periods (a start date and a number of weeks) to pause the whole production at once. A hiatus pushes whatever phase it falls inside outward so that phase still delivers its full requested week or day count — it doesn’t eat into the work. Hiatus weeks appear as a full-width “Hiatus” band. Type a name at the top of a hiatus card to label its band, and click the color square to color the whole hiatus, in both views and every export; the color follows it if you change its dates. A hiatus’s name and color are set on its card only: double-click its band in Waterfall view to go straight to the card.

Notes (in the preview)

The Notes column auto-fills key milestones inline — e.g. “Start Principal Photography 11/02/26”, “Principal Photography Wraps”, union holidays, and any simultaneous-post flags. Each phase’s start and end can be added too, your own custom phases included (“Color Grading Begins 7/5/27”): tick them in Settings › Preferences › Automatic notes.

The two views own their notes separately. Waterfall notes are the master set: they appear in the Waterfall, the Excel export, and the Month view. Month view notes — added by hovering a day and clicking a + — belong to the Month view and its PDF only, and deliberately do not appear in the Waterfall or the Excel export. Every day block shows at least four lines, and each free line has its own +, so a note goes exactly where you click rather than always dropping to the bottom. A note stays on the line you added it to. If a day needs more room than the phases leave, the wider + on the bottom edge of the block adds another line — to the whole week, since the seven day blocks share one calendar row — up to a maximum of six. A block always grows to fit its actual content, so nothing is ever hidden even past that maximum.

Every month prints on exactly one page, filling the sheet. Each page is pinned to the paper and the week rows divide it between them: an empty row still gets its four lines, so a sparse month prints as uniform full-size rows rather than a small grid floating at the top. A row carrying extra comments takes proportionally more of the page and the others give way, so everything stays visible and the calendar always spans top to bottom. If the grid lines print faint or missing, switch on Background graphics in the print dialog’s More settings. Waterfall notes can be edited from either view — editing one in Month view updates the Waterfall and the Excel export too, since it’s the same note. Because a Waterfall note covers a whole week, that editor shows the week’s whole text, so the other notes in it aren’t lost. In Waterfall view, double-click a note cell (or click it and press Enter, or just start typing) to open a small editor beside it — it floats over the calendar, so the grid keeps exactly the shape it had while you type. Type to replace it. The editor says what the cell holds: Auto Note or Holiday when it is just one of those, with a Hide Auto-Note or Hide Holiday button at its top right; a cell holding several lines lists its automatic notes and holidays under the box, each with its own Hide. Hide takes it out of the Waterfall only, at once (the Month view keeps it), and saves anything else you typed. A note you typed has Delete Note at the editor’s top right instead, in either view: in the Waterfall it deletes what was typed in the cell and keeps its automatic notes and holidays, and in the Month view it deletes the one note you clicked. One Undo brings it back. Automatic notes (“Start Principal Photography 1/4/27”) can be reworded and stay automatic: change the words, keep the date, and the note keeps its own day and moves with the schedule, under its new name everywhere it shows. In the Month view, clicking one opens it as an Auto Note, with its own colour and a Hide Auto-Note button, and a small ↻ before it marks it as automatic (a holiday has a ⚑). Clearing an automatic note hides it from the view you cleared it in, and it stays hidden when dates move. Settings › Preferences › Automatic notes chooses which milestones the calendar writes, and in which view: each has a Waterfall box and a Month box, as a holiday does, so a note can show in one view, or both. Writer’s Room Opens and Production’s start and wrap show in both to begin with, and each phase’s start and end (“Post Begins 7/5/27”), your own phases’ included, once you tick them. An empty note loses its highlight. Because a waterfall row covers a whole week, its editor has a Day dropdown. Picking a day stamps that date into the note text — “Table Read” becomes “Table Read 11/04/26” — matching how the automatic notes are written. The date is ordinary text you can reword or delete, and it’s what places the note in Month view; switching days rewrites it rather than adding another. Leave the dropdown on “Mon (default)” and the note simply sits on that week’s Monday. Under it, Stays with keeps a note with a phase instead of a calendar week: choose “Production wk 2” and the note moves whenever Production does — a new start date, Build Around, Shift, the ▲/▼ arrows, a hiatus — and stays on Production’s second week, on the same day. Leave it on the week and the note stays where it is. A note whose phase gets shorter waits on the phase’s last week. The Month view’s note editor has the same Stays with, under the text box. On a shoot day it offers “Production · Day 7”, and the note then follows that shoot day wherever the shoot moves. Its Show in waterfall switch keeps a note that stays with a phase in the Month view only; one you add in the Month view starts with it off. Dragging such a note to another day keeps it with its phase when the phase runs that week, and makes it a plain note of that day anywhere else. Notes added in Month view are pinned to the day you clicked, and each keeps its own highlight colour. The editor also shows the ten standard Microsoft Excel colors — pick one to change that individual cell’s highlight color (text flips black or white automatically for readability). Press Tab or Ctrl/Cmd‑Enter to save, Esc to cancel, or just click away. Reset Notes, at the right end of the top bar, returns every waterfall note to its automatic text and default colour. A hidden automatic note stays hidden: tick its box again in Settings › Preferences › Automatic notes to bring it back. In the Month view the same button reads Reset Month Notes and clears only the notes added there. Hiatus bands have their own Reset hiatus bands, under the All-phase hiatus list. (To clear the whole calendar instead, start a New one.)

Styling text. The Text bar under the toolbar styles any text in the Waterfall. Click a date, a heading, a phase week, a hiatus band or a note to pick it — drag across cells, Shift-click or ⌘-click to pick several — then make it bold or italic, change its colour or alignment, or set its size from 6 to 12. Those sizes always fit a row, so styling never changes the calendar’s shape or how it prints. Click a header line to style it the same way, in either view. The styles are saved with the calendar and appear in the Excel and PDF exports.

Moving around, and moving notes. Once something in the Waterfall is highlighted, the arrow keys move the highlight a cell at a time, and Shift with an arrow stretches it. Tab and Shift-Tab move right and left. An empty Notes cell is a stop, so you can arrow to a week and start typing. Delete (or Backspace) empties the highlighted notes and leaves dates, phases and hiatus bands alone. An automatic note or a holiday emptied this way is hidden from the Waterfall only, so it stays in the Month view (and a holiday keeps its day off). ⌘C, ⌘X and ⌘V copy, cut and paste notes. A copied note keeps its colour, size and style, and it pastes into Excel or an email as plain text. Text copied from anywhere else pastes too: each line goes into the next week down, and one line pasted over several highlighted notes fills each of them. To move a note, highlight it, then drag it to another week. Several highlighted notes move together. A note that stays with a phase keeps it when you drag it to a week that phase runs in, and becomes a plain note of the week anywhere else; a pasted copy is always a plain note of the week you paste it in. If a week already has a note, you’re asked before it is replaced, and an automatic note replaced this way is hidden from the Waterfall. Each of these is one step for Undo. Right-click a cell for a short menu of what that cell can do: start or end a phase in that week, add a phase or a hiatus there, cut, copy, paste or clear a note, remove a hiatus, or see that week (or a note’s day) in the Month view.

Column headings. Double-click any heading in the Waterfall — Date, a year or Notes — to type your own. ← Merge and Merge → join a heading with the one beside it, Split gives each column under it a heading of its own, and Reset puts it back. Headings never widen a column: a long one shrinks to fit, and the Excel and PDF exports show the same headings. Over a Notes column the editor also offers Hide column: a thin strip stands in for it on screen, it is hidden in the Excel and PDF exports too, and its notes stay saved. Click the strip to bring it back.

Sizing the grid (columns, rows & how far a cell reaches)

Columns and rows. Hover a column boundary or the bottom edge of a row in the Date column and drag. Text inside resizes itself to fit: a narrowed column shrinks its labels, and a row’s height sets how many lines a note may use before it is cut off with an ellipsis. Every row starts at the same default height, and while you drag one it snaps to the default and to any height you have already set elsewhere — the handle turns green when it locks on — so rows end up matching rather than a pixel apart. Double-click a boundary to go back to automatic — the column fits its widest entry again, the row returns to the default height. Column widths and row heights are shared with the Excel export and the PDF, so what you size on screen is what prints.

Phases that overlap share the width evenly. In any week where two phases run at once they get half the phase area each; three get a third each, four a quarter. All the phase columns in a year block are the same width, so an even split really is even. A phase running on its own still stretches across the whole area.

Where a phase goes. Columns lay themselves out: a phase that starts the week another ends follows it into that column, and so does one that starts up to four weeks later, when no column has just come free; Production takes the left-hand free column, with Simultaneous Post directly to its right and Post continuing that lane afterwards; anything else goes to the right of whatever is still running. Where a phase could go in more than one column, it takes the one that leaves the year the fewest columns, even if that means Post starts under Production instead of continuing the Simultaneous Post column. Within a year, columns run left to right by when the phase at the top of each started. A calendar saved before this (5 Nov 2026) keeps the layout it was saved with until you take Update layout on the strip above it — nothing moves on its own. Dragging a block into a free column still wins. A phase you move — a new date, its ▲ / ▼, Shift or a new length — keeps the column it was in whenever its new dates still fit there, so nudging it a week never sends it to the other side; where it can’t fit, it goes where the layout puts it and comes back when you move it back. Reset Columns lets the layout place it again.

How far a cell reaches. A phase cell widens into the empty column to its right from the week that column is free for the rest of the phase’s run, whatever runs beside it; a phase alone fills the width; and the Simultaneous Post column is kept for the shoot until it ends. A phase that takes over a column the week another ends keeps that phase’s width while the columns beside it stay empty; once another phase moves into one of them, it keeps to what is left until it ends. A column that holds something beside another phase for only a week or two does not count toward that share, so the phase beside it spreads into it. In Single Column Mode every cell stays one column wide. (A calendar saved before 5 Nov 2026 keeps the old rule — free for the phase’s whole run — until it is updated.) Double-click a cell and its phase fills the empty columns beside it, every week, from then on: it narrows the week another phase moves in, widens again the week it leaves, and follows every shift, so there is nothing to tidy when the calendar changes. Double-click a cell that is already wide and its phase pulls back to its own column, every week. Double-click the cell’s edge to let the layout decide again. If you would rather no phase changed width partway through, switch off Fill Gaps, left of Side Boxes in the toolbar: every phase then keeps one even width for the year, as wide as the space free for its whole run there, in the calendar and its exports. A phase you double-click to fill still widens week by week. Reset Columns, in the top bar beside Reset Notes, does that for every column at once: each phase’s fill or pull-back, every dragged width, and every swapped or moved column go back to the automatic layout, while dates, notes and row heights stay. One undo brings them all back. To set one cell to an exact width instead, hover its left or right edge and drag it across the empty space; the edge snaps to column boundaries and a purple outline shows where it will land. That applies to that one cell in that one week — every other row is left alone. Rest the pointer on empty space beside a phase and a dashed outline marks the weeks where that space sits beside it, with Expand? in the middle: click it and the phase widens across that space in those weeks only. Rest it on a cell that has been widened and Pull back? outlines the space it took; click it to give that space back (for a phase set to fill, it turns the fill off). A phase’s own hiatus counts as part of the phase: the outline runs through it, and expanding, pulling back or double-clicking to fill widens or narrows its hiatus weeks with the rest. Each click is one undo. All of it carries into the Excel and PDF exports.

A width you drag out while a cell has the row to itself is not kept once another phase moves in beside it — that week goes back to the even split, since a cell three columns wide next to a neighbour of one reads as a mistake. Widen it again with the overlap on screen and it stays, because then it is clearly what you meant.

Several cells at once. Rather than doing that cell by cell, drag across a run of cells in the preview to highlight them — phase cells and per-phase hiatus bands alike, in one column or several, across as many weeks as you like. Shift-click extends the highlight to another cell and ⌘-click (Ctrl-click on Windows) adds or removes one. Then double-click any highlighted cell (or press Enter), and every phase in the highlight fills its free space from then on, in a single step, or pulls back to its own column when the highlighted cells are already wide; the label above the highlight says which of the two it will do. Esc clears the highlight, and one undo reverses the whole batch rather than one cell at a time.

Swapping two phases’ columns. Where two phases run side by side, you can trade which one sits on the left. Highlight a cell of the phase you want to move — ⌘-click one, or drag across a run of them — and a small teal circle appears on the boundary beside it. Click the circle — or drag it across the boundary, if you prefer to see it move — or press Alt+← / Alt+→, and the two phases exchange columns for every week they run alongside each other — one step, one undo. Weeks where the phase runs on its own aren’t touched: they have nothing to trade with. To move a phase’s whole run in a year, hover it and click Swap Column at the top of the run; the button appears only on a phase that has something to swap with. Nothing about the phases themselves changes — same dates, same durations, same labels, same widths — only which column each one occupies, and the Excel and PDF exports follow. A swap stays put when you move either phase afterwards: the two keep the order you gave them, even once the one you moved starts first. To let the layout choose again, swap them back, or use Reset Columns.

Two phases can be swapped however little they overlap — the shared weeks move, and the weeks where either phase runs on its own stay where they are, because they have nothing to trade with. Some swaps are still declined, and the app says which and why rather than moving something unexpected: it will not change how many columns a year needs, it will not change any column’s width, and it will not shift a week you didn’t highlight by more than one column. One consequence is worth knowing about, because it is the common one: moving a phase out of a column can let it widen in the weeks above or below, where the column beside it is now free for its whole run. That is shown in amber before you let go. After Swap Column, if the whole column can’t move but some of its weeks can, the circle turns amber and a dashed box shows the weeks that will swap. Those weeks move on their own, so a phase ends up in two columns. Hover the circle to see which phase, and why the whole column can’t move. Production’s column can’t be moved while Simultaneous Post is switched on, since that marker is anchored to it.

Adjusting dates (moving the calendar around)

Above the preview sit two tools: Shift (its ← 1 wk / 1 wk → buttons move the whole calendar one week at a time, and Shift ▾ between them opens the Shift box) and Build Around. Shift keeps the gaps between phases; Build Around closes them. Everything you’ve typed onto the calendar travels with it — notes, highlight colors, and hiatus labels all keep the phase week they were written for, rather than staying behind on the old date.

The Shift box is a list of your phases with a tick box on each: a ticked phase moves and its row says Moves, an unticked one Stays. It opens with every phase ticked, which moves the whole calendar; the ← 1 wk / 1 wk → buttons are the one-click version of that. Untick a phase to leave it behind, and the gap beside it opens or closes. Click a tick box to tick or clear one phase, or press on a row and drag up or down to tick or clear a run of them at once; the row you start on decides which. The box at the top of the list ticks every phase. Once every phase is ticked it shows a minus, and a click clears them all. The line beside it counts how many move. Clicking a row, anywhere but its tick box, chooses that phase without changing its tick: it gets an outline, and the two buttons under the list name it. Prior to … ticks that phase and every phase above it; After … ticks it and every phase below it. Each replaces the ticks you had. How far: By weeks (type a number and press Earlier or Later — the direction of travel, not which phases move) or To a date, which takes a landmark — the start or the end of a phase — and moves it onto your date. The phase that lands is named right above the date, so the two read together: Shoot — starts on — your date. It is the phase you chose in the list, and the box offers only ticked phases, since a phase that stays cannot land anywhere. With every phase ticked the plan keeps its shape and every phase keeps its lead time, and the box also offers Whole schedule: pick it with ends by for a delivery deadline. The two edges behave slightly differently on purpose: a start lands exactly on the week you pick, while ends by is one-sided — work finishes on whatever weekday it finishes, and shifts move in whole weeks, so it lands on or before your date rather than overshooting a deadline to get closer to it. After … leaves the earlier work exactly where it is, so the gap in front of the phase stretches or shrinks — that’s the choice for “the shoot slipped but prep is already booked.” Prior to … is its mirror, for “delivery is fixed, but the shoot has to start two weeks earlier”: the phase moves whole, with its own notes and any hiatus inside it, and the phases after it stay. The list runs in the order the phases start, so a Writer’s Room that runs into Pre-Prep sits above it and stays put with After Pre-Prep; tick it as well if it should come along. Notes go with the phases: with the ticks you set yourself, a note moves when its week is inside a ticked phase’s run. Earlier and Later move the same set of phases either way, and the ticks are forgotten when the box closes.

Build Around is the one that answers a date rather than just moving to it. Shift moves the plan and keeps the gaps between phases; this one builds it, end to end, from each phase’s length — which is why it can write dates into fields that were empty. Its box works like the Shift box: a list of your phases with a tick box on each. Click a row to pin that phase: its row is outlined, and Pin to a date under the list names it. Give it a date — starts on, or ends by for its last workday — and the ticked phases are laid out around it, the ones before it backwards and the ones after it forwards, in one go. So “the shoot starts 6/22” tells you when the writers’ room has to open. Each row shows the date that phase would get and how far it would move, and nothing changes until you press Build. Click a tick box to tick or clear one phase, or press on a row and drag up or down to tick or clear a run. The box at the top of the list ticks every phase; once every phase is ticked it shows a minus, and a click clears them all. What is ticked is what gets built, on both sides of the pinned phase; to build only one side, untick the phases on the other. An unticked phase keeps its dates, and the others are built past it. A phase that runs alongside the one it would be built against — a Writer’s Room that overlaps Pre-Prep, a Casting beside Prod Prep — starts unticked, because building it in line would pull the two apart. A line under the list names it, and you can tick it if that is what you want. A length can be typed right in the list, and is saved with the dates when you press Build; Production’s length comes from Show info and cannot be changed here. A phase that straddles a locked hiatus starts earlier rather than losing weeks. Building backwards through Production works too, and is the one case that isn’t simple subtraction: the shoot has no week count — its length is a day-by-day walk that skips weekends, hiatus days and every enabled union holiday — so how many weeks it occupies depends on where it lands. Rather than run that walk in reverse, the tool searches the real schedule for the latest start that still finishes in time, which means a back-solve can never disagree with the dates the calendar shows.

To move one phase on its own, use the ▲ and ▼ inside its date box, on its card in the Phases tab, in the Waterfall view. Each click moves that phase one week earlier or later and leaves every other phase where it is, so the gaps either side of it change. It takes its own hiatus and its cell settings with it; typed notes, holidays and all-phase hiatuses stay. A run of quick clicks is one undo. Alt+↑ and Alt+↓ in the date box do the same.

Two things deliberately stay put. Union holidays never move — they’re real calendar dates — so shifting the shoot by exactly a week can move its wrap by more or less than a week as it slides into or out of a holiday week; the tools report where the wrap actually landed. And a note with a date in it stays on that date, since it’s about that specific day. All-phase hiatuses are Locked in place by default for the same reason — a winter break belongs to Christmas, not to the schedule around it — so uncheck that lock on any hiatus you want to travel with the plan. Per-phase hiatuses always travel with their phase. Any adjustment can be undone with ⌘Z.

Waterfall view vs. Month view

Each view has its own header with its own Auto/Manual switch, and the two are independent — taking the month header manual leaves the waterfall header alone, and vice versa. In Auto the lines fill themselves from Show Info; switch to Manual and they become an editable snapshot you can word however you like.

Toggle at the top of the preview. Waterfall view mirrors the Excel export — a week-by-week grid with editable notes — and is the default. Month view is a day-by-day calendar where phases run as bars across the days they cover; Production shows as individual episodes.

Getting around the Month view. The strip above the Text bar is a map of the whole calendar: every month, with each phase drawn as a bar under its name. Click a month to go to it, or click a phase to go to the month it starts in. To step a month at a time, use ‹ and › at the right end of the Text bar’s line: the month between them is the one on screen, and Today goes to this month. The dot marks this month, a red mark is an all-phase hiatus, and the faint month at each end is the empty month before and after the phases. A long calendar scrolls sideways inside the strip. The strip stays put when you scroll or zoom the calendar, and it shows only in the Month view.

What sits on top in the Month view. Where phases overlap, the Month view stacks them by start date. To change that, hover a bar and drag the six-dot grip near its left end up or down: the phase keeps that place in every week, on screen and in the PDF. To go back, right-click a bar and choose Back to date order. Notes move on their own day, and you drag the note itself: up or down among that day’s notes, between two phases, above the bars or below them (a bar the note now sits above drops one line for that week, and the notes on the other days stay where they were). Drag a note sideways or to another week to move it to that day: a date in it that names its old day changes to the new one, and a note from the Waterfall moves into that week’s Waterfall note with its new date. Holidays stay on their day. A click that doesn’t move still opens the note. Dragging the middle of a bar still moves its dates, and double-clicking a bar opens its phase’s card in the Phases tab. Whatever you drag, a copy of it follows the pointer while the calendar underneath shows where it will land, and one undo takes the whole drag back.

Exporting

In Month view the button becomes “Export Calendar to PDF.” It writes the PDF and asks where to save it. Every month from the first phase to the last prints, one per landscape Letter page, in full colour with the header, month and date. On screen the Month view’s grid lines are drawn lighter; the PDF keeps its black lines.

Export PDF in Waterfall view first asks three things: the paper (Letter, Legal or Tabloid), with Letter or Legal marked Recommended for this calendar, the orientation, with the automatic choice marked Recommended and roughly how large each one prints the calendar, and the grid lines. The paper and the orientation are saved with the calendar, so Export to Excel uses them too; the grid lines stay on this computer. Bigger paper prints a long or wide calendar larger.

Generates a styled .xlsx matching the Waterfall view: one column block per year, colored phase cells, the milestone Notes column, and a bold printed header with the title, date, and production summary. Columns are sized tight to their content, and the whole grid is scaled to print as large as possible on a single sheet. Orientation is chosen automatically — calendars of two years or fewer print portrait, three or more years print landscape — unless the other orientation would fit noticeably larger, or you chose one when exporting the PDF. The workbook is set to print on the Paper chosen in Settings (US Letter unless you change it), centered on the page, with the print area pinned to the grid, so File → Print → Save as PDF straight out of Excel comes out the same for everyone regardless of their default printer. The file name uses your show title (e.g. “Show Title - Season 1 Planning Calendar.xlsx”).

Files, saving & loading

All the main actions live in the toolbar at the top: the file menu (showing the calendar you’re currently in), New, Save, Save As, Export to Excel, and Reset.

Save writes a small .sptcal file holding all your entries (title, dates, phases, custom phases, hiatuses, edited notes, header mode, and current view). In Chrome or Edge the first save asks where to put the file, and every save after that writes straight back to that same file with no dialog. Load the saved file later and everything comes back exactly as you left it. (A self-contained copy of the whole tool with your calendar baked in is still available as Export App With Data, under Settings → Calendar.)

New clears everything and starts a blank calendar. Save As is different — it copies the calendar you’re working on into a new file and switches you to it, which is handy for forking a schedule to try a variation without touching the original.

The file menu lists calendars you’ve saved; click one to switch to it, use Load… to pull in a calendar file that isn’t listed, or the × to drop a file from the list (that removes the shortcut only, never the file itself). Loading a file again may show a quick one-click permission prompt (“Let this site edit the file?”) — that’s the browser protecting your disk. The file menu and in-place saving need Chrome or Edge; in other browsers each save downloads a new copy instead.

Double-click a .sptcal file to load it straight into SPTCal. The first time, Chrome asks whether to open it in SPTCal — turn on Remember my choice to skip that next time. On Windows, right-click the file and choose Open with → SPTCal (and Always) once. If SPTCal is already open, the calendar loads into that window, with the same unsaved-changes question as Load…. A double-clicked file may ask permission to change it the first time you press Save; until you allow it, it can’t autosave. Older .html calendars still load through Load….

Autosave & recovering work

The indicator beside Export shows Unsaved changes or the time of your last save. Once a calendar is linked to a file, it autosaves every 10 minutes in the background — no dialog, nothing to click.

Work that hasn’t been saved to a file yet can’t autosave (browsers won’t create a file without you choosing where it goes), so the app keeps a rolling backup in your browser’s local storage instead. If a session ends with unsaved changes, the next time you open the app it offers to recover that work. Work on a saved file comes back into that file: the file menu shows its name, and Save writes to it (it may ask permission first). Closing the tab with unsaved changes also triggers your browser’s “leave site?” warning.

The backup lives only in this browser on this computer — it’s never uploaded anywhere, and clearing your browsing data removes it. Treat it as a safety net; the saved file on your disk is still the real copy.

Reset

New clears all your entries and returns every setting to its default state. It also starts a new file, so the next Save asks where to put it instead of writing the blank calendar over the one you had open. Narrower resets: Reset Notes in the top bar (Reset Month Notes in the Month view), Reset Columns beside it in the Waterfall view, Reset hiatus bands under the All-phase hiatus list, Reset holidays in Settings → Region, and Auto in the Header menu, which returns the header to live auto-fill.

Keyboard shortcuts

The file actions have the usual keys. Each one does exactly what its button does, including asking first when it would replace unsaved work. On Windows, use Ctrl where these say ⌘.

  • ⌘N — New
  • ⌘S — Save
  • ⇧⌘S — Save As
  • ⇧⌘E — Export: the Excel file in the Waterfall view, the PDF in the Month view
  • ⌘P — the current view’s PDF
  • ⌘Z / ⇧⌘Z — Undo / Redo

You won’t find them in the Mac menu bar: SPTCal runs inside Chrome or Edge, and the browser builds that menu itself. Its File menu still shows ⌘N beside New Window, but in SPTCal that key starts a new calendar. To open a second window, choose New Window from the menu.

Tip: any date you type snaps to the Monday of its week, and all durations are honored in full even when holidays or hiatuses interrupt them.
